newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Fear and greed stir small-cap Malaysian stocks.
newsitem.headline: Fear and greed stir small-cap Malaysian stocks.

text.p: Fear and greed are pushing Malaysia's small-capitalisation stocks, which have soared to one new high after another in defiance of logic or gravity, analysts said.

Fear of being left off the Second Board index's meteoric ride -- it has more than doubled in value since the end of 1995 -- and greed for fast, easy profits are driving the bull run, the analysts said.

From trading just under the 300 level at the end of 1995, the index reached yet another all-time high on Thursday of 632.64 in early trading. But fear got the better of greed and the Second Board plunged 3.25 percent to 605.11 at mid-day.

"For me, the Second Board is pure psychology, greed overwhelming fear coupled with the huge access to liquidity in a simple demand/supply equation," said Laurence Lau, director of research at local brokerage Jupiter Securities, in a recent commentary for clients.
Supply of Second Board stocks is often limited, making it easy to exaggerate price movements.

Since late August, the Second Board index of nearly 200 stocks with market capitalisations of 40 million ringgit ($16 million) or under, has been on an almost daily trek to uncharted ground, fuelled by a diet of rumours and retail buying.
It has been Asia's second-best performing bourse this year, nudged out only by China's Shenzhen A shares.

Because of its breathless ascent, the Second Board has overshadowed the much better-known, and bluer-blooded Composite Index of 100 of Malaysia's biggest and most well-capitalised firms, which is up about 13 percent from the end of 1995.

"Many investors were frustrated by the stagnation of stock prices in the main board and switched their investments to the Second Board," said Patrick Lim, president of the Malaysian Investors' Association, in a recent market assessment.
"We expect it to outperform the main board for the rest of this year and next year," Lim predicted.

Speculation about asset injections, restructurings, government and project contracts is among the factors driving Second Board share prices. The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange frequently has to issue letters to companies asking them to disclose any corporate development affecting their shares.
Some players also believe the bullish run may be part of fund-raising activities connected to next month's party elections of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation.
Syndicates of local and foreign money are also rumoured to be involved in boosting share prices.
Whatever the reason, many analysts see the Second Board as overpriced, noting its price-to-earnings multiples are about three times those on the main board.
"I've generally been telling people if they want to be involved in the Second Board and they want to trade it, to not be overexposed," said PB Securities research manager Razani Radzi.

An analyst with a local research house sounded a more ominous note: "I think the risk is building up. It's a time bomb. Most of the Second Boards are way above fundamentals even with asset injections and project injections."
